# Clavicle fracture

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Surgery > Trauma and orthopedic surgery > Upper extremity > Clavicle fracture*

[Original Article Link](/library/i30JRf)

---

## Summary

<u>Clavicle</u> <u>fractures</u> are common, especially in children and <u>adolescents</u>, and often result from a direct fall onto the shoulder. They are classified by location using the <u>Allman classification system</u>, with two-thirds of <u>fractures</u> located in the midshaft. Patients typically present with <u>signs of fracture</u> such as swelling, focal tenderness, and reduced arm mobility, or more specific signs such as shoulder drooping or <u>skin tenting</u> around the <u>clavicle</u>. Diagnosis is confirmed with <u>x-ray</u>, although additional imaging studies such as <u>CTA</u> may be needed for suspected vascular injury. Treatment is based on <u>fracture</u> location and may include <u>conservative fracture management</u> and/or <u>surgical fracture care</u>.

---

## Epidemiology

* Common (accounts for ∼ 2.6% of all <u>fractures</u>) [[1]](/library/FSXgYB)

* Most commonly occurs in children and <u>adolescents</u>  [[2]](/library/8SXOYB)

* Most common <u>birth trauma</u> in <u>newborns</u> [[3]](/library/uSXpYB)




Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Etiology

* Direct trauma (∼ 95% of cases) [[4]](/library/ESX8YB)

* Fall onto the shoulder (most common cause), e.g., from bicycle accident

* Direct blow to the <u>clavicle</u>, e.g., from a football tackle

* Indirect trauma (∼ 5% of cases): mainly falls onto an outstretched hand [[4]](/library/ESX8YB)

* <u>Birth trauma</u> (see “<u>Birth-related clavicle fracture</u>”)

---

## Pathophysiology

A midshaft <u>fracture</u> is the most common <u>clavicle</u> <u>fracture</u> because it is the thinnest segment of bone and lacks ligamentous and muscular support. [[5]](/library/Thd6Wp0)

---

## Clinical features

* <u>Signs of fracture</u>, e.g., <u>pain</u>, <u>ecchymosis</u>, swelling

* Sagging of the shoulder due to downward distracting force of the weight of the upper limb on the <u>lateral</u> <u>fracture</u> fragment

* <u>Skin tenting</u> over the <u>clavicle</u> due to the upward distracting force of the <u>sternocleidomastoid</u> on the <u>medial</u> <u>fracture</u> fragment

* Shortening of the <u>clavicle</u> due to the <u>medial</u> distracting force (<u>adduction</u>) of the <u>pectoralis major</u> on the <u>lateral</u> <u>fracture</u> fragment

## Diagnosis

### Clinical evaluation [[5]](/library/Thd6Wp0)[[7]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




Any findings that suggest <u>neurovascular injury</u> or an <u>open fracture</u> should prompt urgent orthopedic consultation.




* <u>Neurovascular examination</u>

* Evaluate for <u>brachial plexus injury</u>, e.g., upper extremity <u>paresthesias</u> or <u>weakness</u>. [[8]](/library/1hd21p0)[[9]](/library/chda1p0)

* Assess for <u>subclavian artery</u> injury, e.g., weak or absent upper extremity pulses. [[9]](/library/chda1p0)[[10]](/library/WhdP1p0)

* <u>Skin examination</u>: Evaluate for <u>laceration</u>, tearing, and <u>skin tenting</u>.

* <u>Lung examination</u>: Assess for <u>signs of pneumothorax</u>.





> [!TIP]
> Posteriorly displaced <u>fracture</u> fragments may result in <u>injuries to the brachial plexus</u>, subclavian vessels, and <u>lung</u> apex. [[5]](/library/Thd6Wp0)




### Imaging [[5]](/library/Thd6Wp0)[[7]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




#### <u>X-ray</u>




* Indication: best initial test for suspected <u>clavicle</u> <u>fracture</u>

* Views: <u>anterior</u>-<u>posterior</u> and 45° cephalic tilt

* Findings: <u>radiographic fracture signs</u>, <u>fracture</u> fragments, displacement, angulation, and/or shortening

#### Additional imaging [[5]](/library/Thd6Wp0)[[7]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




* CT upper extremity or chest: for assessing associated injuries, intraarticular <u>fractures</u>, preoperative planning for complicated <u>fractures</u>, and inconclusive <u>x-ray</u> findings

* <u>CT angiography</u> upper extremity or chest: for suspected vascular injury [[10]](/library/WhdP1p0)

* <u>MRI</u> upper extremity: to assess intraarticular or <u>ligamentous injury</u> and <u>soft tissue</u> structures in high-grade acromioclavicular separations to guide management decisions [[11]](/library/Jidssp0)

* <u>Ultrasound</u>: may be used for suspected pediatric <u>clavicle</u> <u>fractures</u> [[12]](/library/fhdkWp0)

## Treatment

### General principles [[13]](/library/jhd_dp0)[[14]](/library/4hd3Vp0)[[15]](/library/khdmVp0)




* Most <u>clavicle</u> <u>fractures</u> are <u>managed conservatively</u>, regardless of their <u>Allman classification</u>.  [[13]](/library/jhd_dp0)

* <u>Surgical fracture management</u> is increasing, e.g., in patients with:

* Young age

* Few comorbidities

* High-energy injury mechanisms

* Midshaft (group I) <u>fractures</u>  [[13]](/library/jhd_dp0)

* <u>Medial</u> (group III) <u>fractures</u>  [[13]](/library/jhd_dp0)

* Concerns about professional impact (e.g., in athletes) or cosmesis





### Initial management [[7]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




* Provide <u>general fracture care</u>, including <u>analgesia for fractures</u>.

* Immobilize with an <u>arm sling</u> for comfort as soon as a <u>clavicle</u> <u>fracture</u> is suspected.

* Identify <u>indications to consult orthopedics for fractures</u>.

* Consult <u>surgery</u> if there is suspicion of an intrathoracic injury (e.g., <u>pneumothorax</u>, <u>subclavian artery</u> injury)

* Arrange prompt follow-up with orthopedics for all patients.





> [!WARNING]
> Rule out concomitant intrathoracic injuries in patients with <u>medial</u> (group III) <u>clavicle</u> <u>fractures</u>.




### <u>Conservative management</u> [[7]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[15]](/library/khdmVp0)




Recommended for nondisplaced, <u>closed fractures</u>




* Immobilize in an <u>arm sling</u> for 4–8 weeks.

* Perform early passive <u>range of motion exercises</u>.

* Avoid noncontact sports for 6 weeks and contact sports for 2–4 months. [[5]](/library/Thd6Wp0)

* See also “<u>Conservative fracture management</u>.”





### <u>Surgical fracture management</u> [[13]](/library/jhd_dp0)[[14]](/library/4hd3Vp0)[[15]](/library/khdmVp0)




#### Indications




* High risk for <u>malunion</u> or <u>nonunion</u>

* Significant displacement

* Shortening > 2 cm

* Severely comminuted

* <u>Open fractures</u>

* <u>Neurovascular injury</u>

* <u>Skin tenting</u>





#### Operative techniques




Depend on <u>fracture</u> location and type and include:




* <u>Intramedullary nailing</u>

* <u>Plate fixation</u>

* <u>Ligament</u> repair: typically for <u>lateral</u> (group II) <u>fractures</u>

## Complications

* <u>Fracture complications</u>: e.g., <u>nonunion</u>, <u>malunion</u> [[7]](/library/AN1Rdh0)

* <u>Neurovascular injuries</u>: e.g., <u>brachial plexus injury</u>, <u>subclavian artery</u> injury

* <u>Lung injuries</u>: e.g., <u>pneumothorax</u>, <u>hemothorax</u> [[7]](/library/AN1Rdh0)

* <u>Thoracic outlet syndrome</u>





![Thoracic outlet syndrome secondary to clavicle fracture](media/nqqacvdr0d8cyx9vyvumh88t.jpg)

Thoracic outlet syndrome secondary to clavicle fracture




We list the most important complications. The selection is not exhaustive.
